chunks: "Both data and program are just bits, so they can sit in any of the memories in the system; what changes is speed, size, and whether it survives power-off.
On a microcontroller, the program normally lives in on-chip flash, which is non-volatile. Constants like lookup tables and strings live there too. Variables live in SRAM.
Initialized globals are a nice example: their starting values are stored in flash, and the startup code copies them into SRAM before main runs, and the uninitialized ones in .
bss are just zeroed. The stack and heap are regions of SRAM.
On a bigger system, like a phone or a PC, the program is stored on disk or flash storage, which is non-volatile and huge but slow. When you run it, the OS loads it into DRAM.
The CPU then pulls the pieces it is actively using into the caches, which are small fast SRAM, and into registers, which are the fastest of all.
You can also run code from RAM if you want speed, like copying an interrupt handler into fast on-chip RAM.
And peripherals are memory-mapped, so some addresses aren't storage at all.
The architectural twist is that a von Neumann machine uses one memory and one bus for code and data, while a Harvard machine has separate ones.
Most chips are a hybrid: separate L1 instruction and data caches, but one shared main memory."
